one_sentence_story: Knocking on Palo Alto front doors in 1966, Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser discovered the 'Foot-in-the-Door' phenomenon — agreeing to display a tiny 3-inch safe-driving sticker two weeks earlier quadrupled homeowners' willingness (from 16.7% to 76.0%) to put a giant ugly 'Drive Carefully' billboard on their front lawn because small unpaid acts quietly rewrite who we believe we are.
so_what_for_you: Turn Foot-in-the-Door on your own goals with tiny unpaid Day-1 identity votes ('1 paragraph written, 5 minutes walked'), and remember when a stranger hooks you with a '10-second street question' that saying Yes to Step 1 NEVER obligates you to say Yes to a giant lawn sign.

jargon_map.plain: dramatic jump in compliance with a large costly request (76% vs 16.7%) after voluntarily performing a tiny initial request two weeks earlier
jargon_map.analogy: sliding a 3-inch wedge in the door that swings it wide open later

jargon_map.plain: viewing your own small voluntary action and updating your self-image ('I'm the kind of citizen who steps up for causes!')
jargon_map.analogy: becoming what you see yourself freely doing

jargon_map.plain: Freedman & Fraser's surprise finding that signing an *anti-litter* petition still nearly tripled *safe-driving* lawn signs from a different stranger
jargon_map.analogy: proof the shift happens at the 'active citizen' identity level

jargon_map.plain: finding that paying someone externally for the small Step-1 favor erases the Foot-in-the-Door boost
jargon_map.analogy: external cash gives an excuse not to update your identity

jargon_map.plain: Cialdini's *Big No to Small Yes* (same person, same minute, reciprocity) vs Freedman & Fraser's *Tiny Yes to Big Yes* (works weeks apart across different people via identity!)
